title: Why do two copies of the same tiger photo look wrong?
description: One tiger picture is copied in five sizes. Three copies look like the real tiger, one looks stretched and one looks squashed, even though all five are rectangles. The video stops on what the good copies kept.
teaching_notes: One idea: resizing can keep a shape or spoil it, and being a rectangle is not the reason. Watch for students who say the squashed copy looks wrong only because it is a square.

video_script.why: Before any ratio appears, the child meets the puzzle that drives the chapter: some resized copies keep their shape and some do not.
video_script.substitution: Digital pictures resized for a screen or a page, where some copies keep the look of the real tiger and some do not.
video_script.anchor: the book's tiger picture, copied in five different sizes
hold_back: width and height changed by the same factor
never_show: the answer that the good copies changed both sides by the same factor
maths_rules: One tiger picture is copied into five rectangles of different sizes.
Three copies keep the look of the real tiger; one is drawn stretched and long, and one is drawn squashed and fat.
All five copies are rectangles; the squashed copy may be nearly square.
No sizes, numbers or symbols are drawn on screen.
The open question: what did the good copies keep that the odd copies lost. It is never answered.
video_script.design: One idea: resizing can keep or spoil a shape. Assumes nothing. No wrong idea is broken. The five copies stay on the stage to the end.
